This is good news for learners who haven’t found a teacher or knowledgeable mentor yet. And it suggests that, even in a formal educational environment, the best teachers are those who promote egalitarianism over hierarchical learning.

My interest in self-directed learning eventually led me to the Brazilian philosopher Paulo Freire, one of the most influential educational theorists of the 20th century. In his impassioned manifesto Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968), he criticised the idea that ‘the teacher teaches and the students are taught … the teacher knows everything and the students know nothing.’ True learning, Freire believed, could be accomplished only ‘through the restless, impatient, continuing, hopeful inquiry human beings pursue in the world, with the world, and with each other.’

One way to describe Freire’s philosophy, Daniel Walden writes, is that ‘the teacher is not so much an authority as a more experienced student.’ This seems like a radical redescription of what teachers are meant to do in the classroom.

More experienced students can show newer ones what it’s like to be generous to your peers and open to new perspectives

Walden is a classicist who began his career teaching the ‘Great Books’: foundational works of Western literature and philosophy, often emphasising Greek, Roman and biblical texts. In a recent essay in The Point magazine, Walden suggests that Freire’s educational approach closely reflects his own goals as a teacher of the Iliad, the Odyssey, the tragedies of Aeschylus and other classical texts – even those he doesn’t know particularly well. ‘My own teaching benefits tremendously from being unable to pretend to any kind of expertise,’ he writes; ‘texts outside my disciplinary wheelhouse have become some of my favourite material to teach precisely because I can explore them alongside my students rather than insisting that I have something they need.’ Of course, Walden isn’t quite like the students he teaches because he’s spent years studying subjects that others are approaching for the first time. But by demonstrating his own intellectual humility and curiosity, he can invite students to embody these traits too. More experienced students can show newer ones what it’s like to be generous to your peers and open to new perspectives. ‘The secret ingredient,’ Walden writes, ‘is not only the syllabus but the intellectual community that is formed.’

Walden’s description resonated with me because I had experienced this myself: an intellectual community that helped me, and my peers, explore new ideas together.

Seven years after graduating from university, I signed up for a philosophy class taught by the poet Zoe Tuck. In our weekly Zoom conversations, Tuck acted less like a superior than a charismatic, encouraging peer. We read Maurice Merleau-Ponty’s Phenomenology of Perception (1945) together, slowly working through passages that exhilarated and perplexed us. Some people in the group had formally studied philosophy, but many hadn’t. Together, we learned to approach the text with the right balance of humility, confidence and curiosity. And we learned, too, what it meant to pursue self-directed learning in a community.

I had moved from the passive experience of reading a book to the more receptive, social practice of discussing it with others. But I wanted an even more active, generative education: I wanted to produce new works and forms of knowledge. In a university setting, this typically takes place when students need to submit a significant project or thesis. Where else could I find models for self-directed learning? This question led me to stories where someone’s intellectual interests helped launch an unexpected creative career. When J R R Tolkien and C S Lewis first met in 1926, neither man had written the novels that made them famous. Instead, Tolkien was a professor in the English department at the University of Oxford, who had published scholarly works in a small niche, and Lewis was a departmental fellow. The two became closer after realising that they both loved reading Nordic poetry, even though it was unrelated to their research.

A formal education is, for many, only the beginning of one’s intellectual and creative life

A year earlier, Tolkien had shown his mentor an epic poem he was working on, inspired by Norse mythology. His mentor wasn’t particularly supportive, and ‘advised him to drop it’, as the sociologist Michael P Farrell notes in Collaborative Circles (2001), his study of creative friendships. Tolkien resolved to keep his poem a secret. But when he worked up the courage to share it with Lewis, he received a remarkably supportive response: warm praise, along with detailed feedback about specific lines. Being encouraged by a peer may have healed some of the insecurities of being rejected by a superior. As Tolkien gratefully observed:

The unpayable debt that I owe to him was not influence as it is ordinarily understood, but sheer encouragement. He was for long my only audience. Only from him did I ever get the idea that my stuff could be more than a private hobby.

The two began reading each other’s drafts in a critique group that eventually grew to seven members. Two widely read and beloved fiction series eventually emerged from this group: Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings (1954-55) and Lewis’s The Chronicles of Narnia (1950-56). Today, both men are remembered for their novels, not their earlier academic careers.

In the first few years of my self-directed education, I envied those who seemed to have the ideal formal education, complete with the right professors, peers and structure. But stories like these helped me realise that a formal education is, for many, only the beginning of one’s intellectual and creative life. I began, slowly but surely, to piece together what my own intellectual life looked like: taking online classes with writers and literary scholars; joining in-person book clubs to deepen my understanding of challenging texts; and finding friends who offered generous, useful feedback on my work.

Relationships like these might be the most important resource for learning something new. You can teach yourself almost anything, it turns out, within a community of encouraging and intellectually ambitious peers.

item.title: A psychological guide to climbing out of debt
item.dc:creator: Vicky Reynal
item.description:
Debt is as much an emotional challenge as a financial one. Follow this therapist’s advice to create a plan that works

- by Vicky Reynal

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
If you’re struggling with debt, you’ll know that it is more than a financial issue. As a psychotherapist, I work every day with people who have ended up in problem debt – debt that is a struggle to manage or pay back, leading to a spiralling financial situation. I’ve seen firsthand how often debt has roots in deeply emotional issues – and I’ve witnessed its emotional consequences.

Many clients have told me they associate debt with being ‘disorganised’ and feeling ‘irresponsible’. They feel shame about what their debt ‘makes them’ and fear that seeking help will lead to them being judged negatively. As a result, even talking about it becomes difficult. Of course, debt can result from irresponsible behaviour, but this is far from always the case. Anyone can end up with problem debt as a result of relationship breakdown, redundancy, illness and other practical hardships. Whatever the root causes, it can be difficult to face.

You may have found that simple tasks like checking your banking app or opening letters from the bank, calling the bank or seeking money advice feel impossible, perhaps out of a fear of judgment or seeing how the debt has grown. But the longer debt goes unaddressed, the worse the consequences – not just financial (the earlier debt is tackled the more options there are), but also emotional. Guilt can turn into a pervasive shame; a small secret kept long can break the trust in relationships. The manageable becomes overwhelming.

So climbing out of debt isn’t just a financial task, but one that requires the emotional capacity to face the fact without collapsing into panic or avoidance; the courage to take action (action breeds confidence rather than the other way round); the curiosity to explore what caused the debt in the first place; and the humility to ask for help.

I have been with clients as they revealed debt to their partners, and slowly rebuilt those relationships. I have heard their relief when they called the bank and were met with understanding rather than punishment. I have seen first-hand how empowered they felt once the barrier of avoidance is broken. Debt feels terminal, but it doesn’t have to be. It is a problem to be faced, not something that defines you.

I help my clients to unpack what led them to this place and also to find a way out of the shame, dread and secrecy that usually accompanies debt. Below are my suggestions for how you too can find the emotional resources to climb out of your debt.

item.title: S P A C E S
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
A filmmaker tries to reconstruct her brother’s faltering experience of time: adrift and without continuity

- Directed by Nora Štrbová

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: To what extent is our identity intertwined with our memory? The Prague-based filmmaker Nora Štrbová explores this hazy terrain in her mixed-media animation S P A C E S. The film is based on the life of her brother Šimon, who developed a brain tumour that gradually eroded his memory before ultimately taking his life in his 20s. Fragmented visual sequences, including reimagined moments from Šimon’s life and an interview with his friend, break apart and blur, evoking her brother’s faltering experience of time – and, by extension, his faltering experience of himself. Inventive and poignant in equal measure, Štrbová’s immersive short finds a deeper meaning and emotional pull through this experimentation.

item.title: What does it really take to be a resilient mother?
item.dc:creator: Sarah Emmerson
item.description:
New motherhood is hard – and a mother’s ability to cope depends on multiple kinds of strength, both internal and external

- by Sarah Emmerson

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
‘I’m just not strong enough to handle it. My mother did all this and she had three kids. I can’t even cope with one. I’m pathetic.’ Andrea* looks down, avoiding my gaze. I can’t tell where she is looking because we are conducting our therapy session online. Most of my sessions with new mothers have moved online: it’s one remnant of the COVID-19 pandemic that has actually helped new mothers, being able to access therapy without having to leave the house. I am guessing that for Andrea, my compassion in this moment probably feels too uncomfortable to absorb. She is sitting in this belief that she is somehow not resilient enough to handle the demands of motherhood, and my heart breaks for her.

I have been thinking a lot about what resilience means for mothers today. It’s a conversation I have with many of my clients, and a lot of the beliefs I encounter are about deficiency – it’s something they do not have, while others seemingly do. When I met Andrea, she’d just had her first baby. Her son was sleeping for only 45 minutes at a time, and her husband was already back at work. She told me she was crying a lot and not enjoying this time with her son. She chastised herself constantly for not just being grateful. She felt stuck in a place where she did not know how to perform, and everyone else seemed to be doing better than her.

Like so many others, she was judging herself against a blueprint of motherhood that feels unachievable in today’s world. The cost-of-living crisis, low maternity pay and childcare costs make it more difficult for women to juggle work and parenting. A plethora of mothering choices – about breastfeeding, nursery, playtime, the right school, etc – have made it easier for mums to feel like one wrong move might determine their child’s future. Additionally, parenting trends over the past few decades have shifted to a form of developmentally conscious mothering that puts the onus on mums to be strong, caring and emotionally stable from day one, an ideal that is fervently propagated by social media.

It requires superhuman strength to always be attuned and reflective in an unsupportive environment, and so many women feel like they are failing the test. When resilience is conceptualised as a character trait that you either have or don’t have, then a mother is likely to think I am either strong like my mother, my grandmother and the other mums I see, or I don’t have what it takes. Andrea fell into this same trap. She compared herself with her mother – who had never really talked about how hard it was to raise children – and felt that she could not live up to the example.

There is an urgent need to redefine what resilience means for mothers. And emerging research suggests there are better ways for mothers, their families and others to look at it.

The ‘resilience portfolio’ model, proposed by the psychologist Sherry Hamby and her colleagues, offers a useful perspective here. Grounded in research on adverse experiences, it describes how a person’s physical and mental health outcomes after adversity might depend on the combination of their strengths and support structures – their ‘portfolio’. Meaning, the more strengths across different domains you have acquired, the more resilient you’re likely to be when exposed to distressing or traumatic experiences.

The beauty of this idea is that it demystifies why some people are able to cope better with distressing events – and it reminds us that strength is something that can be built. A person’s resilience portfolio is made up of four domains:

  • meaning-making, with aspects such as having hope and a sense of purpose;
  • regulatory strengths, including the ability to reflect on and manage one’s feelings;
  • interpersonal resources, especially the availability of helpful social support; and
  • environmental context, such as access to nature and support structures.

For many women, new motherhood seems to almost systematically dismantle the portfolio of strengths that they previously relied on, starting with the domain of meaning-making. Many women today find identity and purpose in their job, as well as their sense of independence and freedom to make choices about their own lives. Motherhood, at least initially, takes that away. Mums are expected to find their meaning in caring for a newborn. Women I speak to are often used to defining themselves through achievement and getting things done but, in a sense, early motherhood is asking them to just stand still. Andrea didn’t think she would struggle with pausing her career to take care of her baby, and she wasn’t prepared for feeling bored and unfulfilled.

Many communities are not well set up to catch new mums when they stumble

The self-regulation part of the portfolio includes the ability to self-reflect, emotional awareness and self-control, and the skill to self-soothe. A significant proportion of new mothers have not had the opportunity to develop these strengths, often because of experiences of emotional neglect in childhood. Moreover, the emotion regulation skills described here involve the brain’s prefrontal cortex, which can be highly susceptible to disruption by hormonal changes and sleep deprivation, both hallmarks of early motherhood. So even if mums are lucky enough to have good self-regulatory skills, those might not be fully accessible when they are needed most. This is why early motherhood is not supposed to be a solo activity.

The interpersonal resources in the portfolio can take many forms, including a supportive partner, parents, in-laws or friends. For many mums today, support networks are smaller and more spread out than in previous generations. And when other people are available, they are not always supportive in the ways a mother needs. When Andrea had her son, her sisters and mother stayed for a few days, but Andrea didn’t experience them as helpful – she felt criticised by her mother, and her younger sisters showed little interest in the baby.

Finally, the environmental domain reflects that we live in our own little worlds that can be helpful or harmful to our wellbeing. For a new mother, relevant factors might include physical access to green spaces, public transport or baby groups. But they could also extend to whether her maternity hospital has knowledge of trauma-informed principles, whether her workplace offers sufficient maternity pay, and whether she has access to affordable childcare. If one of these resources is missing, it’s likely that others are, too.

Looking at motherhood through this lens might seem bleak, but it is important to acknowledge that many communities are not well set up to catch new mums when they stumble. The ‘strong mother’ myth – you’re either a resilient mother or you’re not – implies that when things feel hard, one is failing, and it ultimately strengthens that self-shaming voice that tells so many women they are not good enough. And few things are as painful as thinking we are not good enough as mothers.

The resilience portfolio also highlights how to have more realistic conversations about what mothers need to bolster their resources. Each domain provides an opportunity for introducing support before, during or after pregnancy.

What worked for Andrea in the end was a mix of multiple approaches, some practical, some more focused on her inner world. Finding meaning in this new experience took time and a lot of self-reflection. We worked on accepting that she enjoyed her work identity and that it did not make her a bad mother to want a career. She had never actively defined her purpose in life, as few of us probably do, but she recognised in therapy that her sense of identity was tied to her ability to fix things and problem-solve, which she had been able to do frequently at work. Not being able to solve her son’s sleeping issues or soothe him when he cried made her feel useless.

Working through this in therapy involved acknowledging that babies are fundamentally unpredictable and uncontrollable. It helped Andrea to find other areas where she could continue to use her problem-solving skills, such as assisting her friend with a home renovation and looking into some more flexible freelance work. For anyone who is in the perinatal period, it is worth thinking realistically about what makes them feel good about themselves, and how they might cope if the usual source of that feeling is taken away, even temporarily.

Mothers need kindness and understanding – from others, and from themselves – to help them recover their ability to regulate

Andrea also needed a larger support system: her interpersonal resources were depleted, and it left little to no time for her to even think about herself. We worked on feelings of guilt and fear that created a barrier to asking for help. She had always been self-sufficient, and it was challenging to realise that she could not do this on her own. She found that she had a few friends who similarly did not have much family support, and they started to check in with each other, which helped her immensely. Finding genuine support during this period means looking for friends or family who feel emotionally safe, whoever they might be. These are often the people who show a genuine interest in a mother’s wellbeing, provide offers of help that take her needs into account and don’t immediately jump in with unsolicited advice.

Andrea was able to find some childcare and use her newfound headspace to feel into herself and reflect on how her life and identity had changed. Not everyone is able to access childcare easily. An important part of the resilience portfolio, environmental variables can be harder to change, but healthcare professionals and families should still take them into consideration. Information about childcare options, charities, playgroups, parental leave, reproductive rights and hospital policies could help new mothers strengthen their resources in this domain.

In early motherhood, things can change quite rapidly. Once her son started sleeping, Andrea felt much more like herself again, and her emotion regulation skills recovered. But these emotional skills can also be built through therapy, and they are among the starting points for cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) approaches. More generally, mothers need early education, especially about the impact of physical factors such as sleep deprivation and hormonal shifts on their ability to regulate their own emotions. And they need kindness and understanding – from others, and from themselves – to help them recover their ability to regulate and self-soothe.

From my work with mothers, I’ve also learned that couples might benefit from asking themselves some questions before their babies arrive, to make sure their resilience portfolios are well resourced:

  • Can you have honest conversations about how you both deal with stress, and what you might need when you’re depleted?
  • How can you make room for baby-free time and address feelings of guilt or shame if they arise?
  • Who are the people you can really rely on for help?
  • What are some of the stories about motherhood that you grew up with?

Early motherhood is hard, and it doesn’t help women to avoid talking about the challenges. What mothers need is more openness and honesty about where they might struggle, and what they – and the people in their lives – can do to make it easier. A mother’s resilience is everyone’s responsibility.

*Andrea’s story is a combination of the experiences of multiple clients; the name and other details have been changed.

item.title: Ask me anything
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
As the Netherlands adopts its strictest-ever asylum policy, Abdulaal Hussein creates space for candid conversation

- Directed by Wyneke van Nieuwenhuyzen

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Filmed in 2024, as the Netherlands was hardening its stance towards asylum seekers, this short documentary follows Abdulaal Hussein, a Sudanese refugee, as he travels the country and holds ‘ask me anything’ sessions with clubs and groups. In these forums, locals – most of them white and native-born – are given the freedom to ask him whatever they’d like about his perspective and life, with Hussein insisting that ‘No question is mean or crazy or inappropriate.’

Observing these meetings as they unfold, the Dutch director Wyneke van Nieuwenhuyzen captures Hussein fielding questions with openness and honesty, his warmth and eloquence seeming to win over each room. She also provides glimpses of Hussein’s life beyond the sessions, allowing us to see him as more than just a spokesperson for refugees. In doing so, more subtle questions emerge about the power dynamics at play: who we are, who we have the right to be, and what we have the right to ask in any given room.

item.title: Journaling to remember
item.dc:creator: Anandi Mishra
item.description:
By cataloguing the ephemera that slip between the headlines of my days, future me has a ready reckoner of my life

- by Anandi Mishra

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
While I’ve come across various literary and artistic works praising the art of looking, what truly led me down this path was Nirmal Verma’s Ek Chithda Sukh (1979), translated as A Rag Called Happiness (1993). In this Hindi novel, the 14-year-old narrator Munnu writes moving descriptions of everyday life in his notebook: ‘This I’ll remember, the boy told himself; I’ll put it down in my diary. Bitty was hanging clothes out to dry. A pale light filled the room. Darry sat back against the wall, his eyes on Bitty …’

Under its influence, I began to narrativise the world around me, so that my journal entries became ready reckoners for the future me: I’d simply page through for what was happening in my life outside the usual things we remember – family, friends, work, city living.

I catalogued the ephemera that tend to slip between the days and the headlines. The dreams I had and probably hated; my thoughts about a bitter cold in the middle of summer; my anxiety before a job interview; the excitement of watching a movie that overwhelmed me.

These are details we tend to gloss over in a 24-hour cycle, but in aggregate they accrue meaning – they slow me down, make me more observant. They denote a sense of time and the self, coming together in a way their digital counterparts don’t. It helps that I journal with pen or pencil, not phone or app, the better to etch the small things in my mind.

At the end of A Rag, all Munnu has are these recollections of times spent with Bitty and her gang of theatre friends over the summer. The break, the year, all these people, pass him by so simply, but the filled-up pages of his notebook, all the observations he has amassed, will stay forever as markings of a time lived – well or not, only time can tell.

item.title: Why long-brewing physical and mental breakdowns feel so sudden
item.dc:creator: Sasi S Senga
item.description:
As a neurosurgeon and a son, I’ve come to see the parallel processes underlying growing tumours and stressed-out minds

- by Sasi S Senga

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
I remember reading the words brain metastases on my phone between surgical cases. As the message arrived, the hospital corridor around me continued its ordinary rhythm. Doors opened and closed. A trolley rattled past toward the next theatre. Somewhere down the hall, a pager sounded and I heard footsteps quickening in response. The axis of my life had been upended but the building around me appeared oblivious.

I read the message again as though repetition might change its meaning. A few minutes later, I washed my hands, retied my mask and returned to theatre. Instruments passed into my palm in familiar sequence: suction, bipolar, clip. My hands followed movements rehearsed thousands of times before.

The tumour had not begun that morning. I knew from my training that, long before those words appeared on my phone, the biological processes that produced them had been unfolding inside my mother’s body.

Since that pivotal day, I keep thinking about the way that collapse often feels sudden, but how rarely that’s the case in living systems. What appears to us as abrupt failure is usually the delayed visibility of strain that has been accumulating for years.

This pattern appears repeatedly across biology and psychology. What looks like stability from the outside reflects hidden systems absorbing strain – what physiologists call homeostasis – until their capacity to compensate is finally exceeded. Systems theorists describe this as movement toward a critical transition. When the threshold is eventually crossed, change can seem abrupt even as underlying instability grows.

Neural circuits possess a remarkable ability to reorganise themselves in response to disruption

Most cancers originate through the gradual accumulation of mutations within individual cells, altering the mechanisms that normally regulate growth, division and repair. Yet the presence of these mutations does not immediately produce illness. Surrounding cells continue performing their roles, the immune system eliminates many abnormal cells, and the architecture of the tissue subtly reorganises itself to preserve organ function. A tumour may therefore grow for years while the organ continues to appear functionally intact. The person carrying it may feel entirely well until that balance is finally exceeded.

In the brain, this dynamic becomes especially striking. Unlike many other tissues, neural circuits possess a remarkable ability to reorganise themselves in response to disruption, sometimes preserving cognition even after profound structural loss. Brain tumours do not merely compress or destroy surrounding tissue. Instead, tumour cells interact directly with surrounding neural circuits, responding to the brain’s electrical activity and integrating into existing networks.

In patients whose tumours infiltrate the language cortex, recordings made during surgery show speech-related activity extending beyond the regions normally responsible for language. As the tumour disrupts the local circuitry, neighbouring networks are recruited to help sustain performance. Language processing therefore becomes distributed across a wider system as the brain attempts to preserve function.

For a time, this redistribution allows cognition to continue functioning normally. Patients may continue speaking, reasoning or navigating their environment even as a disease progresses within the structures that support those abilities. Only when the system can no longer redistribute that burden does the disruption become suddenly obvious.

The brain’s response to sustained psychological pressure follows the same principle. As stress hormones reshape activity across the brain, control gradually shifts away from networks centred in the prefrontal cortex, which support flexible reasoning and deliberate decision-making. At the same time, hippocampal systems that normally provide contextual memory become less influential. In their place, greater influence shifts toward circuits associated with habit and routine, particularly within the striatum.

Crucially, these changes rarely feel pathological at first. On the contrary, they often appear as discipline or productivity. Under chronic stress, you might work longer hours, concentrate more intensely on urgent responsibilities, and postpone activities that don’t seem immediately necessary. Because your outward performance is preserved, the underlying strain remains largely invisible, both to you and those around you.

It was during a stressful period of life that a doctoral student eventually came to see me in clinic, worried that something might be wrong with her brain. Over recent weeks, this young woman had experienced a series of small but unsettling lapses. Midway through a research presentation, she’d lost the thread of her argument and struggled to continue, despite knowing the material well. On another occasion, she missed a familiar turn while driving home along a route she had taken hundreds of times before, and for several seconds could not understand why she was on the wrong road.

Too often, strain is absorbed by those who are more vulnerable and least able to resist it

Rather than interpreting these experiences as due to stress or exhaustion, she began to imagine neurological explanations. Perhaps there was a tumour growing silently. Perhaps the lapses signalled the early stages of cognitive decline. The possibility of a hidden lesion seemed more plausible to her than the idea that her working conditions might explain the change. In medicine, we are trained to look for disease inside the body; it is often harder to recognise the ways environments can reshape how the mind functions.

Thankfully, her imaging was entirely normal. There was no mass, no oedema and no structural abnormality that could account for the symptoms she described. From a neurological standpoint, the scans were reassuring. Yet the experiences that had frightened her were real, and they required explanation.

When she later described the months leading up to these episodes, her story began with a meeting that was supposed to be routine. Her supervisor had suggested it, saying the director of graduate studies would attend to clarify expectations. At first, the conversation seemed procedural. They thanked her for coming and spoke about standards, competitiveness and the importance of maintaining momentum.

As she described the meeting to me, what stood out was how the senior academic’s language gradually shifted. Delays in my patient’s progress were described as ‘patterns’. Questions she had raised about supervision were reframed as signs of her ‘dependency’. No one raised their voice, but by the end of the meeting, the challenges of the doctoral programme had somehow been reframed in terms of questions about her resilience. You might have seen these dynamics yourself. In hierarchical institutions, strain rarely travels upward to those in power. Too often, it is absorbed by those who are more vulnerable and least able to resist it.

In the wake of the meeting, my patient told me how her sleep shortened, meals became irregular and how she’d given up leisure activities to devote more time to her studies. Her attention narrowed toward immediate demands and, for a time, the strategy worked. Those lapses that frightened her were the first signs of the strain becoming visible. They marked the moment when a nervous system that had been compensating for too long could no longer sustain the effort.

After I’d reassured her that there was no evidence of a tumour or degenerative disorder, the true explanation for her symptoms became easier to consider, though not necessarily easier for her to accept.

However, several months later she returned briefly to the clinic to thank me. She mentioned how, after the scans, things had begun to improve. With encouragement from family and friends, she’d made small adjustments: reduced some commitments, restored a more regular pattern of sleep, and gradually reintroduced routines that had once structured her days but had disappeared during the months of greatest pressure.

A mind that had been compensating for too long had begun to regain its equilibrium

The improvements were gradual. Tasks that had once felt disproportionately demanding slowly returned to their familiar scale. Reading, concentrating and speaking no longer felt such an effort. Conversations unfolded without the need to rehearse sentences internally before speaking. The small cognitive hesitations that had alarmed her began to recede.

Listening to her describe these changes, it sounded to me like her cognitive flexibility was returning. Her attention had widened again, making it easier to hold multiple ideas in mind and move between them without effort. What looked like renewed motivation was in fact the restoration of regulatory capacity. A mind that had been compensating for too long had begun to regain its equilibrium.

My patient’s experience can be understood from an evolutionary perspective. The tendency of living systems to compensate rather than immediately fail reflects a fundamental biological and psychological priority: survival in the present moment often takes precedence over preserving optimal function across the lifespan, even if this means damage accumulates over time. Continuing to function despite accumulating strain can be more advantageous than signalling distress too early.

The same principle operates across many levels of biology. Cells continue dividing despite accumulating mutations if doing so preserves tissue integrity. Neural circuits recruit neighbouring regions when networks are compromised, and psychological systems narrow attention toward urgent demands when environments become overwhelming.

When I received the message telling me that my mother had developed brain metastases, it felt like a dividing line between one life and another. Yet what stayed with me was not only the diagnosis itself, but the realisation that it had arrived so late in the story. By the time those words appeared on my phone, the disease had already been shaping her life for months, perhaps years, while her body continued to adapt in ways neither of us could see. The news felt sudden; what it revealed was anything but.

That realisation altered the way I thought about apparent stability. Over the years, I found myself returning to that same observation in many different settings. Not because cancer and psychological strain are the same phenomenon, nor because they arise from identical biological mechanisms, but because both reveal something fundamental about living systems: the work required to preserve function is often least visible when it is succeeding.

Understanding this does not allow us to foresee every collapse before it occurs. It may, however, change what we pay attention to. The earliest signs of strain are often easy to overlook because they arrive disguised as ordinary adaptations. Life becomes increasingly organised around what feels necessary. What is urgent begins to crowd out what is restorative, and the resulting narrowing can easily be mistaken for dedication, productivity or resilience.

Seen in this light, care involves more than responding to visible distress. It also means attending to what is gradually disappearing: opportunities for rest, moments of curiosity, sources of connection and renewal. The things that give life depth, texture and meaning are often the first things surrendered in the effort to keep going.

Perhaps this is why collapse so often feels sudden. What we witness is not the beginning of a failure but the culmination of a long period of accommodation. We notice the moment a structure gives way, not the years it spent holding itself together.

item.title: The full-service grandad
item.dc:creator: Liam Heneghan
item.description:
I thought I was a present father; my sons said otherwise. When my granddaughter arrived I made an offer

- by Liam Heneghan

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
The grandmother hypothesis is well known. Grandmothers are said to improve evolutionary fitness, helping children survive and families endure across generations. I know a grandma who carries a spare diaper in her handbag. Then there’s the grandfather effect. According to some anthropologists, grandads reduce the survivorship of offspring. When a grandad mooches around, his sons have fewer kids. We snooze, we’re odiferous, we eat too much – right out of the mouths of babes! But if science has been slow to celebrate us, life has recently handed me a counterargument. Three years ago, when my granddaughter came home from the hospital, I committed myself to becoming what I now call a ‘full-service grandad’.

I too had grandfathers. One, called Danda, daily consumed fried bread and loved his rashers of bacon. He would run with me up and down the length of Xavier Avenue in Dublin’s North Strand, and when the trains pulled out of the station, we paused to wave, up, up, up so high on the bridge at the end of that short street. The other grandfather, Grandy, smoked his pipe, or rather he prepared his pipe, shaving the plug of tobacco, stuffing the bowl, striking the match, and raising it aloft as he talked till it burned down to his fingers. His background was revolutionary, storyful, pious; the memories linger a half-century after he is gone.

Even before I became a grandfather, I looked the part. My hair greyed in my 30s and then whitened; my beard is billowy and snowy. My complexion, though not quite rosy, is a little pinkish. December is a cruel month for men embodied in this way. This year, a young man crossed over from his line to mine in Trader Joe’s to announce that I look like Santa. It was the 7th of January. ‘Christmas is over, friend,’ I said. ‘I’ve reverted to being Karl Marx.’ He shrugged, unrepentant, as they always are. But in the main, I look like a generic grandad. Even before my granddaughter was born, children glanced up at me with timid recognition. My granddaughter is now three, and I have grown into the role. Despite ongoing requests from her grandmother – Yiayia – I won’t cut my hair or shave: ‘Why upset the child?’ By genetics, by age and by a natural joviality, I am a fully gestated grandfather.

When my granddaughter was bundled up and readied for her homecoming from the hospital to her first apartment in Lincoln Square in Chicago, I travelled behind the main party by train and walked the chilly street from Ravenswood to join the family. It is a route I’ve walked hundreds of times since. I had committed to being a full-service grandad. The offer had been made and accepted: I was to be a caretaker for two full days a week for as long as her parents needed me. I had, I think, been a very present dad to our two boys. And yet, years before my granddaughter was born, I expressed to the family – everyone was home for the holidays – ‘Wasn’t it great that, because I’m a professor, I could be home so much when you were small?’ How everyone laughed that day. When the chortling subsided, a son had mopped his eyes, he said: ‘You were never around.’ Had I missed out, I wondered? Maybe. One thing I do know about family life now: despite how arduous and all-consuming it is, no matter how tired you feel, that phase is over too quickly. I am a full-service grandad, and yet I realise there is a clock ticking on that service.

Does a full-service grandad change diapers? Yes, he does. This is perhaps the first question a prospective full-service grandad might ask. I recall that this delicate question was on my mind when, just a few weeks after she was born and my ‘training day’ was complete, it was just her, me, and a really quite unpleasant deposit. Was I really up for this, I wondered. But yes, it’s part of the deal. I have since changed – by my back-of-the-envelope calculation – 686 diapers and then pull-ups over the past three years. The child is now potty trained, but I sometimes glance at the last of the pull-ups on her bedside table and wonder when a diaper might have my name on it – a geriatric question for another essay. So much for diapers. But just as importantly, I have overseen feedings, nap times, tummy time, library visits, stroller jaunts and, above all, park visits, playground romps, river walks, bird-watching, squirrel-noticing, beach days, and a full immersion in nature. This is what I am here to say: the full-service grandad does all the routine labours of care, but must also ask what distinctive contributions he brings.

There is something incomparable about offering what you have while they are still so young

I had promised myself that I would not turn my granddaughter into a project. It is tempting, as an ecologist, to observe her too closely. But what interests me most is not what she reveals as a subject, but what she helps me see again. Yes, yes – that is a sparrow, a doggie, a worm, a hawk in a tree, a puddle worth splashing in. The success of my method lies in the fact that young children and elderly gentlemen alike take everything slowly. I will not make a study of her, and yet by catering to her attention I’ve learned how to see the world with fresh wonder.

Each full-service grandad must discover his own talent. Mine is to immerse my granddaughter in the green and leafy world – an intense exposure she might not otherwise have had, at least not so early. Who knows what the future holds for this tiny child who has braced herself against Chicago’s bitter winter days, leapt wellington-booted into spring-swollen puddles, and ambled along sunbaked sidewalks with a floppy hat pulled low? She knows the moored boats along her stretch of river and pauses to remark on the geese drifting across North Pond. She knows her goldenrods, her butterflies, her asters. She never fails to notice the sky. The urban outdoors will have left its mark. And each grandad brings his own gifts: familiarity with the beasts of the countryside, an eye for the stars, a mechanical mind, a musician’s ear, or a facility with art. Imparting these gifts is not the work of an idle afternoon; they require time, patience, and presence. Grandads in the traditional mode may well shine later in a child’s life, but there is something incomparable about offering what you have while they are still so young. Committing to being a full-service grandad begins with a simple act of self-interrogation: what part of the world can I open for this child?

I am a full-service grandad, but it’s a lonely task. I am often the solo grandad in the library, the park, and at the beach. There is, of course, a well-documented crisis in childcare: it is expensive for a parent to stay at home, expensive to send children to daycare, and expensive to hire a carer. And though grandparents often step up – my granddaughter is in the exceptional care of my daughter-in-law’s mother two days a week, and Yiayia, more often than not, shares the responsibility with me now that she is retired – even those contributions come at a cost. We are all finite beings, of course, but finitude feels more urgent in one’s 60s than when one is 20: time engaged in one pursuit means less time for others. I still work full-time, so time not spent with her is fully consumed by paid work. I have written less, applied for fewer grants, and postponed conference-going. My years with my granddaughter have cost the world at least one book and two or three essays. That’s at least a few hundred people deprived of desultorily glancing over my prose. It is both a cost and a very great privilege to do the work of a full-service grandad but, gendered norms being what they are, very few of us are availing ourselves of this opportunity. I want to see more grandads in the fray. Let us nod to one another as the kids throw a hundred pebbles into Lake Michigan – a slight salute in the Nature Museum’s butterfly haven. We have been an evolutionary mixed bag for far too long; it’s time to redress the historical imbalance.

On creaky legs, hoist yourself from your easy chair, Grandad. Apply a final touch of pomade to thinning hair and place that hat firmly upon your head. We shall skip stones on the lakefront; place block upon block in the children’s corner of the library; push strollers through the streets and encourage toddling steps upon the grassy hills of our parks. We shall never surrender that little hand when crossing a busy street. There is no crisis of loneliness in the Brotherhood of Full-Service Grandads, only a surging confidence in our mission. Grandads of the world, we have done well – but now we must do better. We have nothing but our naps to lose, and a world to set right: a little child to care for.

item.title: The end of humanity
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Instead of accepting that humanity will soon be obsolete, we can build a better future with respect for human traditions

- A film by Andreas Dürr and Jan-Marc Furer

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
A choir of tech titans and influential commentators has grown inescapably loud with proclamations that technology will soon render humanity, in its current form, obsolete. This leaves each of us with a binary choice: embrace the coming ‘post-human paradigm’ or get left behind. Created by the Swiss filmmakers Andreas Dürr and Jan-Marc Furer, The End of Humanity pushes back against the idea that we can, or should, be so easily replaced. Integrating cinematic sci-fi flourishes and interviews with philosophers, theologians and other leading thinkers, the documentary argues that corporate incentives, a compliant press and a fundamental misunderstanding of humanity itself have pushed conversations about the future towards fatalism. Instead, the film makes the case that the future is far from settled: we needn’t eschew technology entirely, but should build it in a way that respects our intellectual traditions, preserves our humanity and, in so doing, engenders a better future.

This short is condensed from a feature-length version of The End of Humanity.

item.title: When you feel moral disgust, what’s the emotion telling you?
item.dc:creator: Brandon Yip
item.description:
Some actions and words provoke instant revulsion. To know if we can trust that gut feeling, we should probe why we have it

- by Brandon Yip

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
‘Disgusting’ and similar words are flung across political divides quite often today. For example, the US president Donald Trump has used the word to describe his political opponents, journalists and others. And many have voiced disgust at the president’s own behaviours. For instance, after viewing Trump’s altercation with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a press conference in 2025, the author David Brooks described feeling ‘nauseated, just nauseated’. In politics and beyond, expressing disgust is a common response to actions that one finds deeply objectionable, such as racist rhetoric, acts of sexual abuse or policies that harm vulnerable people.

Rather than see expressions like these as merely rhetorical, many philosophers and psychologists argue that moral disgust is a distinct and significant kind of moral response. The distinction between moral disgust and regular disgust lies in the way their objects are experienced by the disgusted person. People feel regular disgust in response to the spread of filth, which motivates physical avoidance and cleansing. The stench of urine on a train, for example, provokes this kind of disgust. When people feel moral disgust, it’s as if they are experiencing a sort of moral pollution, which motivates them to socially avoid and exclude the target of the disgust. Betrayal and exploitation, for example, often provoke moral disgust, but not regular disgust.

Many scholars believe that disgust operates based on simplistic and unreliable heuristics. For example, in his book Yuck!: The Nature and Moral Significance of Disgust (2011), the philosopher Daniel Kelly argues that disgust is an evolutionarily old mechanism that protected humans from poisons and parasites – and so it operates on a ‘hair trigger’ that is prone to generate false positives. Kelly thinks that, since moral disgust grew out of regular disgust, it is similarly unreliable when it comes to moral matters. Just as you can find some physical thing disgusting (say, a certain kind of cheese) when it’s actually harmless, you might automatically find some behaviours morally disgusting that, on reflection, aren’t so bad.

Now, some of Kelly’s premises can be challenged: there is evidence that our emotional systems are intelligent and adaptable. Rather than just recapitulating ancient functions, our emotions contain updating mechanisms that enable them to respond to new physical and social challenges. Furthermore, even regular disgust is flexible and remarkably sensitive to context. For example, whether you find saliva disgusting depends a lot on whether it comes from your lover or a total stranger.

Some have argued that, far from being unreliable, moral disgust plays an invaluable role in moral judgment. In Leon Kass’s classic essay ‘The Wisdom of Repugnance’ (1997), he claims that people’s disgust towards human cloning gives us some reason to avoid that practice, warning us ‘not to transgress what is unspeakably profound’. In this decadent age, Kass says, ‘repugnance may be the only voice left that speaks up to defend the central core of our humanity.’

So, is feeling morally disgusted by an act or a practice something that we should take seriously as a sign that it is morally problematic? To answer this, we need to first get clear on why people feel moral disgust – what exactly it alerts us to.

Contemporary philosophers have offered various explanations of what moral disgust does, though each of these has limitations. In Alexandra Plakias’s account, for example, moral disgust is a response to behaviours that are socially contagious: norm-violating behaviours, such as acts of physical violence, that might spread through a population if left unchecked. This is a compelling idea, but upon further examination, the relationship between socially contagious behaviours and moral disgust appears to be tenuous. Many norm violations that could be socially contagious – such as stealing office supplies or not declaring tips as taxable income – don’t tend to strike people as morally disgusting.

Presenting a different view of moral disgust, Victor Kumar suggests that it’s a response to behaviours that undermine relations of trust and reciprocity. He is certainly right that behaviours that undermine cooperative relations, such as betraying one’s compatriots or unfairly dividing rewards, are often seen as morally disgusting. Yet there are also many other acts that people find morally disgusting – such as cannibalism, or incest among consenting adults – that do not involve a failure of reciprocity.

Imagine you’re in a soccer game with players who are randomly picking up the ball and throwing it around

I believe that John Kekes was on the right path with a suggestion he put forth in the 1990s. Kekes proposed that moral disgust enforces moral taboos – prohibitions against the kinds of actions that endanger the very possibility of civilised life. These violations supposedly ‘threaten to bring about a form of life in which moral considerations have no foothold.’ This seems somewhat overblown: after all, civilisations have repeatedly survived the violation of moral taboos. But perhaps what moral disgust does is guard against the collapse of particular forms of rule-structured life.

To see what I mean, consider the relationship between our personal behaviours and the social worlds that we inhabit. A social world is structured by rules and norms that people have internalised and adopted. Tamar Schapiro points out that these normative orders are sustained by individuals’ compliance with the rules. A judge who continues to follow legal procedure – even when they could choose to act corruptly – helps to sustain the larger normative structure that gives the judge’s actions legitimacy.

If norm compliance keeps important social structures intact, then perhaps certain actions can undermine them. Imagine that you are trying to play soccer with players who are randomly picking up the ball and throwing it around. Such behaviour not only violates the rules of the game, it undermines the game itself. Something analogous happens in typical cases of moral disgust, where the stakes are higher. In explaining his nausea at seeing Trump behave ‘vilely’ toward Zelenskyy and US allies, for example, Brooks suggested that Trump was unravelling a benign, US-centred international order and replacing it with one where ‘might makes right’. Let’s call actions that undermine a social order socially corrosive.

My proposal, then, is this: moral disgust is a response to behaviour that is socially corrosive. More precisely, when some behaviour undermines a set of moral norms that a person is attuned to, they feel morally disgusted.

The moral norms you are attuned to are those that appear to you to impose genuine constraints on behaviour. Your attunement to these norms might be strong and overt – you might explicitly endorse your culture’s norms against using corporal punishment on children, for example. Or, your attunement might be merely implicit. If you grew up in an Islamic culture that sees eating pork as morally disgusting, but then you left Islam, you might still continue to experience the pork prohibition as having some force. People can also become attuned to new norms. An adult Muslim convert – or a vegan – could come to acquire moral disgust towards pork-eating.

Behaviours once seen as morally disgusting, such as premarital sex, are now widely seen as acceptable

When I suggest that morally disgusting actions undermine some social order, I mean that they threaten to stop a community from operating with some set of moral norms. For example, if a political leader engages in corruption or an employer openly flirts with his employees, then the norms that govern that society or that workplace will be undermined as long as such behaviour goes unchecked. This possibility is more serious than just contagious norm-violation; it is not simply that more corruption or more creepy flirting is forthcoming. It’s that the rule of law or respectful workplace interactions become tenuous altogether. Moral disgust alerts us to the fact that certain behaviours might corrode the moral norms that we care about, and it motivates us to sanction or exclude those who behave in those ways.

With this in mind, it is worth returning to Kass’s article about cloning and disgust. He notes that human beings have ‘systems of identity and relationship on the bases of … deep natural facts of begetting,’ and suggests that cloning would confound ‘all normal understandings of father, mother, sibling, grandparent, etc.’ To Kass, then, what is problematic is not just the wrongness of cloning in itself or its mere proliferation. Rather, accepting cloning would unravel a set of norms governing human relations.

Could cloning really undermine all that? It’s not as implausible as it might seem. Already, the norms surrounding sex and the family have undergone radical transformation over the past century. Behaviours once seen by many as morally disgusting, such as premarital sex or homosexuality, are now widely seen as morally acceptable. This has produced profound changes in the meaning of marriage and sex. Even if we consider these changes liberating – welcome alterations to an overly constricting social order – these examples show how it’s plausible that a broader set of moral norms (such as those structuring families) is susceptible to change once key norms (such as those governing procreation or sex) become undone.

Clearly, we should not uncritically endorse the deliverances of moral disgust. One may, for example, decide that the familial structure that Kass protects is an unjust and patriarchal one. The norms we are attuned to are a mixed bag that includes both aspirational ideals that bend towards justice, as well as the nastier parts of our cultures.

Yet it is still worth listening to our moral guts – carefully. Moral disgust sometimes provides a signal that something is deeply wrong, even when one’s capacity for moral reasoning has been compromised. Ditte Marie Munch-Jurisic has noted, for example, that the perpetrators of heinous crimes often react with disgust toward their own actions. Under the Nazi regime, some soldiers and citizens experienced sheer revulsion in carrying out their role in the Holocaust. They suppressed this revulsion with reasons provided by the ideological narratives of the Nazi regime. Similarly, Miranda Fricker has shown that injustice sometimes makes it hard to understand the conditions of oppression. For example, prior to acquiring the concept of sexual harassment, many women struggled to articulate the problematic nature of men’s inappropriate advances. But they were morally disgusted by such behaviour, even before they could fully explain why it was wrong – including how it undermined norms of equal respect for men and women.

If there is a wisdom in moral disgust, then, it is an ambivalent one that we should not always heed, yet cannot simply ignore. Unfortunately, there isn’t a simple formula to tell us whether moral disgust is highlighting something important or leading us astray. When we feel or encounter moral revulsion, we should neither dismiss it as mere primitive reaction nor treat the emotion as having an infallible moral authority. Instead, we ought to pause and reflect on what we are actually responding to. We should try to articulate the normative order that our revulsion is guarding – and then ask ourselves whether or not we have good reasons to cherish it.
